title: Erewhon: or, Over the Range
description: Published anonymously in 1872 and one of the most original satires in English: the account of an imaginary country discovered beyond a mountain range, whose institutions invert those of Victorian England.
plot_or_argument: Higgs, a sheep farmer, crosses the range into Erewhon, where he finds a society in which sickness is a crime and crime is treated as illness, where the churches are 'Musical Banks', where 'hypothetical' language is forbidden, and where the 'Book of the Machines' records the debate on whether machines might become conscious and should be abolished. He falls in love with Arowhena and escapes with her in a balloon.
principal_characters: Higgs; Arowhena; Yram; Chowbok (Kahabuka); the Nosnibor family; the Professors
historical_context: The 1860s-70s, Darwinian theory, the machine age, the Victorian criminal law and the treatment of the insane, and Butler's own experience of New Zealand sheep farming.
literary_significance: Erewhon is the first English novel to treat the possibility of machine consciousness seriously (its 'Book of the Machines' anticipates the literature of artificial intelligence) and one of the sharpest satires on Victorian institutions; 'Erewhon' (nowhere) and 'Erewhonian' entered the language, and the book influenced Huxley, Orwell and the modern dystopia.

title: The Way of All Flesh
description: Written between 1873 and 1884 and published posthumously in 1903: the most complete fictional indictment of the Victorian family, and the novel that made Butler a hero to the generation of Shaw and the Edwardian critics.
plot_or_argument: The novel follows four generations of the Pontifex family, from the tyrannical clergyman Theobald and his son Ernest, through Ernest's miserable childhood, his disastrous marriage to Ellen, his imprisonment for attempted assault, and his eventual inheritance and freedom, to the narrator Overton's amused commentary on the whole.
principal_characters: Ernest Pontifex; Theobald Pontifex; Christina Pontifex; George Pontifex; Alethea Pontifex; Overton; Ellen; Dr Skinner; Towneley
historical_context: The 1830s-50s, the Victorian clergyman's household, the public school and the university, the law and the church as careers, and the social constraints on women and children.
literary_significance: The Way of All Flesh is the central English novel of Victorian family tyranny and one of the founding texts of the modern anti-Victorian reaction; its ironic narrator and its biological view of character influenced the Edwardian novel of the 'new woman' and the twentieth-century family novel, and it is the classic fictional statement of Butler's theory of hereditary habit.
attribution_notes: Published posthumously in 1903, nineteen years after it was written and the year after Butler's death; the text was prepared by R. A. Streatfeild, and Butler had left instructions that it should be published.

title: Life and Habit
description: Published in 1877, the first and most important of Butler's books against Darwin: an argument that heredity is a form of memory, that the embryo 'remembers' the habits of its ancestors, and that life is a series of unconscious recollections.
plot_or_argument: Butler argues that personal identity is continuous through the generations, that the development of the embryo is an act of memory, and that the 'variations' on which natural selection depends are themselves the result of effort and habit rather than random accident.
historical_context: The 1870s, the Darwinian controversy, the 'provisional' theory of pangenesis, and the debate on instinct and inheritance in the new biology.
literary_significance: Life and Habit is the founding text of the modern idea of the 'selfish gene' era's opposite — inherited memory and unconscious habit: Butler's theory influenced Bergson, the early twentieth-century biology of Hering and Semon, and the modern discussion of epigenetics and the inheritance of acquired characteristics. It is the central English contribution to the anti-Darwinian argument of the nineteenth century.

title: Erewhon Revisited Twenty Years Later, Both by the Original Discoverer of the Country and by His Son
description: Published in 1901, the year before Butler's death, and his own sequel to Erewhon: the return of Higgs's son to the country where his father's visit has become a religion.
plot_or_argument: John Higgs returns to Erewhon and discovers that his father's arrival and departure have become the basis of a new religion, 'Sunchildism', complete with a fraudulent priesthood, a 'Mahaina' goddess and a new set of musical banks; his attempt to explain the truth is suppressed by the professors.
historical_context: The 1890s, the comparative study of religion and the 'higher criticism' of the Bible, the growth of the Victorian imperial cult, and Butler's interest in the 'historical Jesus' controversy.
literary_significance: Erewhon Revisited is the classic English satire on the origin of religions and on the priestcraft that preserves them: it anticipates the modern sociology of religion and the fictional treatment of the historical Jesus, and its portrait of a belief system founded on a misunderstanding is among the most sophisticated in Victorian satire.

title: The Woman in White
description: Serialised in Dickens's All the Year Round from November 1859 to August 1860 and published in three volumes: the first and greatest English sensation novel, and the book that made the phrase current.
plot_or_argument: Walter Hartright, a drawing master, meets a woman dressed in white on the road to London and learns that she has escaped from an asylum; he goes to Limmeridge House to teach the half-sisters Laura Fairlie and Marian Halcombe, and Laura is married to Sir Percival Glyde, whose secret is an illegitimacy that invalidates his title. Glyde and Count Fosco confine Laura in the asylum in place of Anne Catherick, the woman in white, who has died; Marian and Walter recover Laura's identity through documents, and Glyde's secret is discovered and he dies in the burning church.
narrative_structure: Multiple first-person narration by the witnesses, assembled as evidence in a case.
principal_characters: Walter Hartright; Laura Fairlie; Marian Halcombe; Anne Catherick; Sir Percival Glyde; Count Fosco; Countess Fosco; Frederick Fairlie; Mr Gilmore; Mrs Catherick
literary_form: Sensation novel (All the Year Round, 1859-60; three volumes 1860)
historical_context: The 1850s, the lunacy laws and the private asylum, the legal position of married women under coverture, the Matrimonial Causes Act of 1857, and the Italian political exiles in London.
literary_significance: The Woman in White is the defining sensation novel and one of the founding texts of the English detective story; its multiple narration, its critique of the legal non-existence of wives and its villain Count Fosco made it the model for the whole literature of mystery and testimony.

title: The Moonstone
description: Serialised in All the Year Round in 1868 and described by T. S. Eliot as 'the first, the longest, and the best of modern English detective novels': the theft of a sacred Indian diamond from a Yorkshire country house, told by a succession of witnesses and solved by Sergeant Cuff.
plot_or_argument: The Moonstone, looted from a Hindu temple by a British officer, is left to his niece Rachel Verinder on her birthday and disappears that night; Sergeant Cuff's investigation, the suspicion of the servants, the devotion of the three Indian priests who follow the stone, and the discovery that Franklin Blake took it in an opium-induced trance lead through a London moneylender and a scientific experiment to the stone's return to India.
narrative_structure: Eight narratives by different witnesses, with a prologue at Seringapatam and an epilogue in India.
principal_characters: Sergeant Cuff; Franklin Blake; Rachel Verinder; Godfrey Ablewhite; Ezra Jennings; Gabriel Betteredge; Rosanna Spearman; Mr Bruff; Mr Murthwaite; Lady Verinder
historical_context: The 1860s, the empire and the colonial looting of India, the new detective police, the professionalisation of medicine, and the Victorian country house and its servants.
literary_significance: The Moonstone founded the English detective novel and established its conventions: the country-house crime, the closed circle of suspects, the professional detective, the chain of evidence and the final explanation. Its colonial subject makes it a central text of postcolonial criticism.

title: No Name
description: Serialised in All the Year Round in 1862: the story of Magdalen Vanstone, left illegitimate and penniless by the discovery that her parents' marriage was invalid, who sets out to recover her fortune by disguise and intrigue.
plot_or_argument: Magdalen and Norah Vanstone lose their name, inheritance and social position when their father's marriage is found void; Magdalen trains as an actress, adopts a series of disguises, pursues the heir Noel Vanstone and his housekeeper Mrs Lecount, marries him, and loses him to death and the will; the novel ends with her illness, her sister's marriage and her own quiet recovery.
principal_characters: Magdalen Vanstone; Norah Vanstone; Captain Wragge; Noel Vanstone; Mrs Lecount; George Bartram; Admiral Bartram; Mr Pendril
literary_form: Sensation novel (All the Year Round, 1862; three volumes 1862)
historical_context: The 1857 Matrimonial Causes Act and the law of legitimacy, the position of the illegitimate child, and the Victorian theatre.
literary_significance: No Name is the most direct Victorian novel about the legal construction of identity: Magdalen's loss of her name is a loss of her legal person, and the novel's argument for the reform of the law of legitimacy is as explicit as anything in the period.

title: Armadale
description: Serialised in the Cornhill Magazine from November 1864 to June 1866: the most complex of Collins's plots, built on a dream, a shipwreck and two generations of the Armadale name.
plot_or_argument: Allan Armadale is warned in a dream by a German doctor that he will meet a man who will be his fate and a woman who will be his ruin. He meets Ozias Midwinter, the son of the first Allan's victim, and Lydia Gwilt, a governess, forger and adventuress, who marries Midwinter in order to murder Armadale; the plot turns on a letter, a sanatorium and a poison, and ends with Lydia's death and Midwinter's survival.
principal_characters: Allan Armadale; Ozias Midwinter; Lydia Gwilt; Dr Downward; Mr Brock; Neelie Milroy; Mr Bashwood
historical_context: The 1860s, the law of the shipwreck and the insurance fraud, the private asylum, and the Victorian fascination with mesmerism and hereditary destiny.
literary_significance: Armadale is the most technically daring of the sensation novels and the one most concerned with the psychology of the adventuress: Lydia Gwilt is one of the great villainesses of Victorian fiction, and the novel's use of the dream and the hereditary curse links it to the Gothic.

title: The Dead Secret
description: Serialised in Household Words in 1857 and the first of Collins's novels to show the full sensation method: a deathbed secret hidden in a Cornish house, and the slow uncovering of a substituted identity.
plot_or_argument: Captain Treverton's wife confesses on her deathbed that her daughter Rosamond is not his child; the confession is hidden in the Myrtle Room at Porthgenna Tower, and the novel follows the servant Sarah Leeson's flight, the search for the letter, and Rosamond's marriage and discovery of the truth.
historical_context: The 1850s, the Cornish setting and its wrecking economy, the Victorian deathbed and testament, and the Household Words readership.
literary_significance: The Dead Secret is the technical experiment in which Collins developed the method of The Woman in White — the hidden document, the withheld identity and the domestic secret.

title: The Haunted Hotel: A Mystery of Modern Venice
description: Published in 1878 and the finest of Collins's shorter sensation works: the story of a Venetian palace, the disappearance of Lord Montbarry, and a dream that reveals a murder to a sleeping woman.
plot_or_argument: Lord Montbarry abandons his fiancée Agnes for the Countess Narona and dies in Venice; the palace he bought becomes a hotel, and the guests are troubled by a smell, a stain and a dream. The Countess's confession reveals that Montbarry was murdered for his money, and the hotel's room yields the evidence.
historical_context: The 1870s, the Venetian tourist industry, and the Victorian interest in dreams and psychical research.
literary_significance: The Haunted Hotel is the most perfect of the English supernatural detective stories and a key text in the literature of the dream as evidence; it was a model for Henry James's later Venetian fiction.

title: The Law and the Lady
description: Published in 1875 and the first English detective novel with a woman as the investigator: Valeria Woodville's campaign to clear her husband of the murder of his first wife.
plot_or_argument: Valeria discovers on her honeymoon that her husband Eustace Macallan was tried for poisoning his first wife Sara, and that the Scottish verdict was 'not proven'. She investigates the case herself, travels to Scotland, interviews the witnesses, and establishes that Sara's death was suicide.
historical_context: The 1870s, the Scottish verdict of 'not proven', the Victorian poison trials, and the position of a wife with no legal standing of her own.
literary_significance: The Law and the Lady is the founding English novel of the female detective: Valeria's investigation is an argument for a woman's intelligence and legal capacity, and the novel's use of the Scottish verdict made 'not proven' a permanent English phrase.

title: Heart and Science: A Story of the Present Time
description: Published in 1883 and Collins's most direct attack on the ethics of experimental science: the story of a vivisectionist who schemes to marry his ward for her money and to use her in his experiments.
plot_or_argument: Dr Benjulia, a vivisectionist, and the physician Dr Gallilee plot to gain control of the fortune of Carmina Graywell; the Italian girl is drugged and detained, and rescued by her cousin Ovid Vere; the novel's argument against vivisection is carried by the suffering of the animals and by Benjulia's suicide.
historical_context: The 1870s-80s, the English anti-vivisection movement and the 1876 Cruelty to Animals Act.
literary_significance: Heart and Science is the central English novel of the anti-vivisection controversy and one of the earliest fictional treatments of the ethics of scientific experiment.

title: The Frozen Deep
description: Written with Charles Dickens in 1856 and performed at Tavistock House in January 1857 with Dickens as Richard Wardour: a melodrama of Arctic exploration, self-sacrifice and the discovery of a rival's worth.
plot_or_argument: Two explorers, Richard Wardour and Frank Aldersley, are rivals for the same woman; in the Arctic, Wardour discovers that the man he is about to kill is his rival and instead carries him across the ice to safety, dying in the effort.
literary_form: Melodrama in three acts (with Charles Dickens)
historical_context: The 1850s, the Franklin expedition and the Arctic searches, and the amateur theatricals of the Dickens circle.
literary_significance: The Frozen Deep is the most famous collaboration of Dickens and Collins, and it shaped the climax of A Tale of Two Cities; it is a key document in the theatrical culture of the 1850s.

title: Modern Love
description: Published in 1862 and the record of the breakdown of the poet's marriage: fifty sixteen-line poems that narrate, in the third person, a husband's discovery of his wife's infidelity and the slow death of their marriage.
plot_or_argument: The sequence follows a husband and wife through the night of the wife's confession, the husband's attempt at generosity, the wife's suicide and the husband's grief; the poems are spoken by a narrator who is neither the husband nor entirely outside him.
literary_form: Sonnet sequence of fifty sixteen-line poems
meter_and_prosody: Fifty sixteen-line sonnets (four quatrains and a couplet), rhymed abba cddc effe gg, with considerable freedom of stress.
historical_context: The 1861 death of Mary Ellen Meredith, the legal position of a wife under coverture, and the divorce law of 1857.
literary_significance: Modern Love is the first English sonnet sequence to treat a marriage from inside and to make the wife's infidelity the subject; it broke the Petrarchan convention of the sequence as idealising worship and made the form available for psychological narrative.

title: The Ordeal of Richard Feverel: A History of Father and Son
description: Published in 1859 and Meredith's first major novel: the story of a father's 'system' of education and the destruction of his son's happiness by the very theory designed to protect it.
plot_or_argument: Sir Austin Feverel brings up his son Richard on a rational 'system' that excludes women and feeling; Richard falls in love with Lucy Desborough, marries her secretly, is separated from her by his father's refusal, is deceived into believing her dead, and the novel ends with her death and Richard's own.
principal_characters: Richard Feverel; Sir Austin Feverel; Lucy Desborough; Austin Wentworth; Adrian Harley; Lady Blandish; Ripton Thompson
historical_context: The 1850s, the Victorian debate on education, the marriage law, and the German and French fiction of education.
literary_significance: The Ordeal of Richard Feverel is the first English novel of education to make the father's system the villain: its critique of rationalist child-rearing anticipates Butler's and the twentieth-century novel of the family.

title: The Egoist: A Comedy in Narrative
description: Published in 1879 and generally regarded as Meredith's masterpiece: the comedy of Sir Willoughby Patterne, a baronet of perfect self-satisfaction whose engagement to Clara Middleton is gradually destroyed by the revelation of his egoism.
plot_or_argument: Sir Willoughby, having been jilted by Constantia Durham, is engaged to the young and intelligent Clara Middleton, who comes to see that his generosity, his taste and his charm are all functions of his self-love. Her escape is engineered by Vernon Whitford, whom she marries, while Willoughby marries the adoring Laetitia Dale.
narrative_structure: Single-location comedy of manners with a chorus of house guests and a narrator who comments as the 'comic spirit'.
principal_characters: Sir Willoughby Patterne; Clara Middleton; Vernon Whitford; Laetitia Dale; Constantia Durham; Dr Middleton; Mrs Mountstuart Jenkinson; Crossjay Patterne; Horace De Craye
historical_context: The 1870s, the position of the educated woman and the marriage market, the English country house, and the Victorian debate on egoism and altruism.
literary_significance: The Egoist is the great English comedy of the ego: its analysis of a self-love that mistakes itself for generosity is a permanent contribution to the psychology of the English gentleman, and its portrait of Clara Middleton is one of the finest studies of a woman's intellectual coming-to-consciousness in the century.

title: Beauchamp's Career
description: Published in 1875-76 and the most political of Meredith's novels: the story of Nevil Beauchamp, a Radical naval officer who stands for Parliament and is destroyed by his own honesty.
plot_or_argument: Beauchamp campaigns for the Radical cause in a Tory constituency, is rejected by the aristocratic Cecilia Halkett, is drawn to the French revolutionary Rosalia (Renée), and is finally drowned while saving a child in Venice; the novel's argument is that his integrity is both his glory and his ruin.
historical_context: The 1867-74 electoral politics, the first Gladstone ministry, the Franco-Prussian war of 1870, and the Victorian debate on the aristocratic versus the democratic principle.
literary_significance: Beauchamp's Career is among the finest English political novels of the nineteenth century and the most direct treatment of Radical politics by a major novelist.

title: Diana of the Crossways
description: Published in 1885 and modelled on the life of Caroline Norton: the story of Diana Warwick, a brilliant Irishwoman trapped in a loveless marriage, whose social ruin and financial self-making made the novel a founding text of the New Woman debate.
plot_or_argument: Diana Merion marries the brutal Augustus Warwick to save her brother, leaves him, is befriended by the politician Percy Dacier, is accused of passing a political secret to the press (she is innocent), and after Warwick's death supports herself by writing novels. She finally accepts the love of Thomas Redworth.
historical_context: The 1880s, the Married Women's Property Act of 1882, the position of the separated woman, the law of libel and the political press.
literary_significance: Diana of the Crossways is the most important English novel of the 1880s on the position of the separated woman and the earning of a living by writing; its heroine is a self-made professional and a central text of late-Victorian feminism.

title: The Shaving of Shagpat: An Arabian Entertainment
description: Published in 1855 (dated 1856) and praised by George Eliot and the Pre-Raphaelites: an Arabian romance in the manner of the Thousand and One Nights, in which the barber Shibli Bagarag must shave the miraculous hair of the tyrant Shagpat.
plot_or_argument: Shibli Bagarag, a barber of the Persian city, is enlisted by the enchantress Noorna bin Noorka to shave the single hair on the head of the tyrant Shagpat, which makes him invulnerable; the quest takes him through a series of magic kingdoms, and the tale ends with the tyrant's fall and the release of his people.
historical_context: The 1850s, the Victorian taste for the Oriental tale (Lane's Thousand and One Nights, 1838-40).
literary_significance: The Shaving of Shagpat is the finest English Oriental prose romance of the century and the work in which Meredith's comic and allegorical gifts first appeared.

title: Far from the Madding Crowd
description: Serialised anonymously in the Cornhill Magazine in 1874 and published in two volumes: the novel that made Hardy famous and the first of the Wessex novels to be set in the fully realised rural world of his invention.
plot_or_argument: Bathsheba Everdene inherits a farm at Weatherbury and is courted by the shepherd Gabriel Oak, the prosperous farmer William Boldwood and the soldier Frank Troy; she marries Troy, who is killed by Boldwood, and after years of widowhood and the ruin of Boldwood she marries Oak.
principal_characters: Bathsheba Everdene; Gabriel Oak; William Boldwood; Frank Troy; Fanny Robin; Joseph Poorgrass; Jan Coggan; Liddy Smallbury
historical_context: The 1870s, the agricultural depression and the decline of the yeoman farmer, the corn market and the harvest.
literary_significance: Far from the Madding Crowd established the Wessex novel and made Hardy a major novelist; its integration of rural labour, landscape and the marriage plot is the model for the English regional novel.

title: The Return of the Native
description: Published in 1878 and the most tragic of the early Wessex novels: the story of Eustacia Vye, the passionate and thwarted woman of Egdon Heath, and of her marriage to Clym Yeobright, the native who returns from Paris to teach.
plot_or_argument: Eustacia Vye, longing to escape Egdon, marries Clym Yeobright, who has returned from the diamond trade to become a schoolmaster; his blindness, the interference of his mother, and Eustacia's rekindled attachment to Damon Wildeve lead to her flight and the drowning of Eustacia and Wildeve in the weir.
principal_characters: Eustacia Vye; Clym Yeobright; Damon Wildeve; Thomasin Yeobright; Diggory Venn; Mrs Yeobright; Captain Vye; Susan Nunsuch
historical_context: The 1840s-70s, the heath economy of furze-cutting, the return of the colonial emigrant, and the Victorian debate on education and the 'native' who returns.
literary_significance: The Return of the Native is the great English novel of the heath and of the woman who is destroyed by place; its opening description of Egdon is one of the most famous in English fiction and its fatalism is the purest statement of Hardy's philosophy before Tess.

title: The Mayor of Casterbridge: The Life and Death of a Man of Character
description: Published in 1886 and generally regarded as the most perfectly constructed of Hardy's novels: the story of Michael Henchard, who sells his wife and daughter at a fair in a drunken impulse and lives to be destroyed by the return of his own past.
plot_or_argument: Henchard sells his wife Susan and baby Elizabeth-Jane at Weydon-Priors fair, swears an oath of temperance for twenty-one years, and becomes mayor of Casterbridge; Susan returns, Henchard's rival Donald Farfrae rises in the town, the wife sale is discovered, and Henchard's fortune, reputation and relationships are progressively destroyed, ending in his death alone in a hut on Egdon Heath.
principal_characters: Michael Henchard; Susan Henchard; Elizabeth-Jane Newson; Donald Farfrae; Lucetta Le Sueur; Joshua Jopp; Abel Whittle; Richard Newson
historical_context: The 1840s, the corn trade and the agricultural depression, the town of Dorchester, and the Victorian debate on character and determinism.
literary_significance: The Mayor of Casterbridge is the classic English novel of character and fate: its wife-sale opening is one of the most famous scenes in English fiction, and its study of a man destroyed by his own past is the purest statement of Hardy's tragic method.

title: Tess of the d'Urbervilles: A Pure Woman Faithfully Presented
description: Published in 1891 with the subtitle 'A Pure Woman Faithfully Presented' and the most controversial of Hardy's novels: the story of Tess Durbeyfield, seduced by Alec d'Urberville, married and abandoned by Angel Clare, and destroyed by the double standard of her society.
plot_or_argument: Tess Durbeyfield, whose family believes itself descended from the Norman d'Urbervilles, is sent to claim kin and is seduced by Alec; she bears a child who dies, works at the dairy at Talbothays, marries Angel Clare, confesses her past on the wedding night, is abandoned by him, is driven back to Alec, and when Angel returns she kills Alec and is arrested at Stonehenge and executed at Wintoncester.
principal_characters: Tess Durbeyfield; Alec d'Urberville; Angel Clare; Joan Durbeyfield; John Durbeyfield; Marian; Retty Priddle; Izz Huett; Liza-Lu; Sorrow
historical_context: The 1880s-90s, the decline of the rural labourer, the evangelical revival, the Victorian sexual double standard, and the publication history of the novel.
literary_significance: Tess is the central English novel of the sexual double standard and one of the great novels of the nineteenth century: its defence of Tess as 'a pure woman' made it the founding text of the novel of social justice for women and a permanent point of reference for feminist criticism.
attribution_notes: First published in a censored serial version in the Graphic (1891) and then in three volumes with the full text restored; the standard text is the Wessex Edition of 1912.

title: Jude the Obscure
description: Published in 1895 and Hardy's last novel: the story of Jude Fawley, a stonemason refused admission to Christminster university, and of his cousin Sue Bridehead, whose intellectual freedom and sexual fear make her one of the most complex women in Victorian fiction.
plot_or_argument: Jude Fawley studies the classics in a village and is tricked into marriage with Arabella Donn; he goes to Christminster, meets Sue Bridehead, and lives with her unmarried after she leaves her husband Phillotson; their children are killed in a murder-suicide that Jude interprets as a judgement, Sue returns to Phillotson in penance, and Jude dies in the rain at the Remembrance Day celebrations.
principal_characters: Jude Fawley; Sue Bridehead; Arabella Donn; Richard Phillotson; Little Father Time; Mrs Edlin; Uncle Drusilla Fawley
historical_context: The 1890s, the university question and the exclusion of the working class, the marriage law, the 'New Woman' debate, and the publication crisis that followed the novel's reception.
literary_significance: Jude the Obscure is the most radical of the Victorian novels on class, education and marriage, and the novel whose reception ended Hardy's career as a novelist. Its critique of the university made it a founding text of the literature of class exclusion, and it stands at the exact boundary between Victorian and modern fiction.
attribution_notes: The serial in Harper's Monthly (1894-95) was heavily cut; the 1895 one-volume edition restored the text and provoked the attack that led Hardy to abandon fiction.

title: The Dynasts: An Epic-Drama of the War with Napoleon
description: Published in three parts between 1903 and 1908 and the most ambitious English verse drama of the modern period: an epic of the Napoleonic wars, from Trafalgar to Waterloo, with the 'Phantom Intelligences' of the Immanent Will commenting on the action.
plot_or_argument: The drama follows the campaigns of 1805-1815 across Europe, with Napoleon, Wellington, Nelson, Pitt and the common soldiers of Wessex as its figures; the Spirits watch from above, and the work ends with the retreat from Moscow and the field of Waterloo.
principal_characters: Napoleon Bonaparte; Wellington; Nelson; Pitt; the Spirit of the Years; the Spirit of the Pities; the Spirit Ironic; the Spirit Sinister
literary_form: Epic-drama in three parts, nineteen acts and 130 scenes
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse for the principal speeches and lyric metres for the choruses, with prose for the domestic scenes.
historical_context: The 1890s-1900s, the new imperialism and the Boer War, and the Edwardian taste for the pageant and the historical spectacle.
literary_significance: The Dynasts is the greatest English verse drama of the twentieth century's beginning and the fullest statement of Hardy's philosophy of the Immanent Will; it is the last English epic.
